profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal design review at a research lab for a near-final paper and demo plan around 'Attention Tracker,' a training-free method for detecting prompt injection attacks by monitoring attention shifts in LLMs. The proposal has already shown promising benchmark results, and the meeting is meant to decide whether the current design supports the paper's core claims and whether the implementation is ready to be included in the lab's shared security-evaluation stack. The agenda is to review claim wording, evaluation sufficiency, implementation assumptions, and readiness for external release. The expected outcome is a decision on whether to approve the design as-is for submission and demo integration, or to request narrowly scoped revisions.

members.name: Dr. Lina Park
members.expertise: LLM interpretability, attention analysis, model behavior diagnostics
members.background: Lina leads a small interpretability-focused project and developed the core Attention Tracker analysis after prior work on attention-head attribution in instruction-following models.
members.private_state: She wants the design review to confirm that the paper's framing is already strong enough for submission and is wary of requests that would expand the work into a systems paper or require a new round of large-scale experiments.
hidden_assumptions: If the detector does not update model weights or train an auxiliary classifier, it is fairly described as 'training-free,' even if there is one-time offline analysis to identify important heads per model family.
The paper's 'small LLM' claim is adequately supported by experiments on 7B-8B open-weight instruction-tuned models because those are standard small baselines in current academic comparisons.
Saying the method 'generalizes across attack types' reasonably refers to performance on multiple benchmark families and held-out attack templates, not to every downstream agent or tool-use setting.

A method can be said to require 'no additional LLM inference' as long as it reuses attentions from the same forward pass, even if serving infrastructure must expose and store per-layer attention tensors.
For a design review, implementation details that depend on standard research instrumentation do not need special discussion unless they affect the core algorithm.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.role: Applied Research Engineer, security evaluation lead
members.expertise: LLM evaluation pipelines, red-teaming, inference systems, benchmark operationalization
members.background: Arjun maintains the lab's attack-evaluation harness and is responsible for deciding whether research prototypes can be reproduced cleanly and integrated into internal safety testing workflows.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid approving wording or design assumptions that will create friction when the method is later ported into the lab's production-oriented evaluation stack, but he also wants to appear supportive rather than obstructive.
hidden_assumptions: If a method is called 'training-free,' it should also avoid model-specific calibration steps, manual head discovery, or offline tuning that must be repeated for each new model.
The phrase 'small LLMs' is most meaningful for deployment if it covers 1B-3B models, since 7B models are still too heavy for many practical edge or embedded settings.

A claim of 'generalizes across attack types' should survive transfer into materially different prompt-injection settings, such as tool-using agents or retrieval-augmented assistants, not just new strings within benchmark datasets.

If a method claims 'no additional LLM inference,' it should impose minimal serving-path overhead and should not depend on capturing full attention tensors that are unavailable or expensive in standard inference stacks.
Design review approval means the proposal is not just scientifically plausible but sufficiently specified for handoff into a shared evaluation framework without hidden integration surprises.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to Attention Tracker as a 'training-free' detector.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the method requires no gradient updates, fine-tuning, or learned auxiliary detector at deployment time; offline identification of important heads is still consistent with 'training-free.'
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the method should require no per-model calibration, head-selection pass, or offline search beyond directly running the target model and reading its outputs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML papers, 'training-free' is commonly used loosely, so both hear a familiar positive property and assume the other is using the standard meaning without probing the operational details.

misalignment_points.topic: Which models the 'small LLMs' claim covers
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the method works well on 'small LLMs.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the 7B-8B open-weight models already included in the evaluation appendix.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of 1B-3B models that matter for constrained deployment and internal lightweight testing.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'small LLMs' is widely used but relative; each participant silently maps it to the model scale most common in their own workflow, so the discussion feels aligned.

misalignment_points.topic: What standard of 'generalizes across attack types' is being reviewed
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the design should support the claim that the method 'generalizes across attack types.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the claim is satisfied if performance remains strong across multiple benchmark datasets and held-out attack templates within the paper's evaluated families.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the claim is only strong enough if it plausibly extends to structurally different attack settings, such as tool-use or RAG-mediated injections, even without retraining.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both endorse generalization as a goal, but 'across attack types' sounds specific enough that neither realizes they are applying different evidentiary thresholds.

misalignment_points.topic: What is excluded by 'no additional LLM inference'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the method is attractive because it needs 'no additional LLM inference.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the claim excludes extra forward passes only; extracting attention tensors from the same run is within scope and therefore free in the sense relevant to the paper.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the claim excludes any materially new runtime burden in the evaluation stack, including heavy attention logging, tensor retention, or custom hooks not present in normal inference.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a narrow compute claim, and because both are accustomed to attention access in research environments, neither initially treats instrumentation scope as a separate issue.

I do not want this to turn into a request for another month of experiments or a systems integration overhaul. If we can leave with approval plus a couple of wording tweaks, that's the right outcome.
